results.title: Last week, I met the founders of CoffeeSpace. Founded by Malaysians building something like a Tinder for co-founders in Silicon Valley. Super inspiring and eye opening! They’ve pivoted once… | Deric Yee Ji Yong | 19 comments
results.content:
Of all the co-founder breakups we see, particularly those that happen early on, at least half happen because the tech co-founder isn't good enough. I don't say that to be rude, I'm just being realistic. Truth is, most technical co-founders end up being someone that the other founder(s) know. This can work. Especially if you went to a top, top school, or have worked in companies with genuinely world class engineering teams and met them there. Being honest though, most of us haven't. And that fact ends up causing a whole range of different problems. The bar for a technical co-founder should be astronomically high. They need to be a phenomenal engineer, fantastic at building and managing teams, and commercially minded in a way that's suitable for an early startup. ^this is 1/1000. It's [...] needed someone who could help get a functional MVP live. Clarity on scope comes before finding your match. 𝟑. 𝐒𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐰𝐡𝐨 𝐈 𝐰𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐝, 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐰𝐡𝐨 𝐈 𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐞𝐝. I pictured a woman founder in edtech, but that narrowed my search too much. What I really needed was someone hungry, reliable, and aligned with our mission. Questions like work style, time zone, and location (visa requirements, etc.) mattered more than I realized. YC’s cofounder questions doc was super helpful for alignment checks. [ 𝟒. 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐦𝐲 𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐧𝐞𝐭𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤. I spent too much time on cofounder-matching sites and not enough looking at my extended network. Even if no one close to you is the fit, your friends of friends might be. 𝟓. 𝐅𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐨 𝐬𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐦𝐲 𝐯𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧. Technical talent has options.   I keep seeing founders playing startup cosplay. - Branded hoodies for a 3-person team. - Welcome kits with custom notebooks. - Posting BS vanity metrics on LinkedIn. ... And zero revenue. You're not building a company. You're acting like one. 6 months in, you've burned through $150k on theater and you're still 'pre-revenue.' Sorry to break it, but: If you don't have revenue, you don't have a company. You just convinced someone to give you money. Real companies are built on customers, not vibes.

results.title: Insights, Tips & Success Stories for Cofounders
results.content: Every one of these eight problems comes down to the same underlying mismatch: startup hiring runs on direct visibility, sourcing, and founder-level decisions, while most of the advice and infrastructure candidates default to was built for large-company, high-volume hiring instead. That mismatch is exactly the gap CoffeeSpace exists to close — putting early hires and cofounders directly in front of the startups actually looking for them, instead of routing every application through a system built for a completely different kind of hiring. For anyone searching for an early-stage role and tired of applying into silence, or a founder trying to find the right early hire without wading through a generic inbound pile, CoffeeSpace is built to make that direct connection happen. [...] the point where the excitement was real, CoffeeSpace is built to close that gap. [...] bet, CoffeeSpace is built to help make that call with real information instead of a name on a slide.
